name: Scott Forstall
milestone_by_age_26: Ineligible: Born 1969; earned Stanford Symbolic Systems B.S. (1991) and CS M.S. (1992), then joined NeXT around age 22–23. Material breakout work—Aqua UI leadership (~2000, age ~30–31), Safari, and leading iPhone software (mid-2000s)—all arrived after age 26. Joining NeXT as a new graduate is early employment, not a material independent milestone of notable success.
early_history_summary: Forstall grew up in Kitsap County, Washington (nurse mother, engineer father; brother later at Microsoft), was Olympic High valedictorian, then Stanford. After co-creating WordArt on a Microsoft internship, he joined Steve Jobs's NeXT in 1992 and stayed through the Apple acquisition, rising later to SVP of iOS.
family_context_summary: Second of three boys; mother Jeanne was a registered nurse and father Tom an engineer; older brother Bruce became a senior software design engineer at Microsoft.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father worked as an engineer and older brother entered software engineering at Microsoft; some family technical orientation is documented, but not a direct product/apprenticeship pipeline.
evidence_summary: Wikipedia and Bloomberg Businessweek establish birth year 1969, Stanford graduation 1991–92, and NeXT hire in 1992. Aqua and iPhone leadership came in his thirties. Early NeXT employment and giftedness in school are real but do not meet the material-milestone bar used elsewhere (e.g., Bezos VP at 26 treated as non-qualifying).

Family domain advantage is strongly documented (both parents CS PhDs/engineers in SV). Later founding of Block Party and TIME recognition came after 26.

name: Charlie Robbins
milestone_by_age_26: Co-founded Nodejitsu, an early Node.js platform-as-a-service company, in April 2010 at age 24 (birthday May 6, 1985) with high-school friends Marak Squires and Paolo Fragomeni, becoming CEO of a recognized Node.js cloud startup.
early_history_summary: Born May 6, 1985, Robbins left a Wall Street path after discovering JavaScript and Node.js, co-founding Nodejitsu in New York in April 2010 with longtime collaborator Marak Squires. He became a prominent early Node.js contributor and open-source evangelist while building one of the first Node PaaS products, later acquired by GoDaddy in 2015.
primary_leverage_engine: Node.js technical depth on rising platform
primary_early_advantage_tags: Node.js wave, high-school cofounders, open-source/npm ecosystem, NYC startup scene
evidence_summary: Nodejitsu Wikipedia and Bloomberg Businessweek date founding to April 2010 by Robbins, Squires, and Fragomeni; We Are NY Tech profile (April 2011) states he was 25 with birthday May 6, 1985, placing founding at age 24. He rode the early Node.js wave as CEO/contributor; company later took Joyent partnership and Bloomberg Beta interest before GoDaddy acquisition (2015).
starting_point: Born May 6, 1985; family background not documented in reviewed sources; entered Node.js ecosystem from a prior Wall Street path in New York.
current_position: Engineer and leader; co-founded Nodejitsu (acquired by GoDaddy 2015); later engineering leadership roles including at GoDaddy; Node.js community figure (indexzero).

trajectory.event: Co-founded Nodejitsu PaaS in April with Marak Squires and Paolo Fragomeni and registered early Node.js cloud brand.
Launched private beta of Nodejitsu platform (~November), becoming one of the first commercial Node.js hosting providers.
Partnered with Joyent on Node infrastructure; Nodejitsu positioned as original Node.js PaaS as Joyent later pointed users to it.
Acquired IrisCouch; Bloomberg Beta investment spotlighted Nodejitsu among early portfolio bets.
Nodejitsu acquired by GoDaddy and exited the PaaS business; Robbins continued in engineering leadership.

name: Theodore Ts'o
milestone_by_age_26: In 1994 at about age 26, created Linux's /dev/random kernel interface and driver—the first Unix-like kernel CSPRNG interface providing high-quality cryptographic random numbers to user programs—while also co-authoring the ext2 design paper the same year.
early_history_summary: Born 1968 in Palo Alto, California, Ts'o earned an MIT computer science degree in 1990 and stayed at MIT Information Systems as Kerberos V5 development team leader. He became an early North American Linux kernel developer (from ~1991) and by 1994 shipped foundational cryptography and filesystem infrastructure still used across Unix-like systems.
secondary_engine: Elite institutional pipeline (MIT); open-source Linux wave
family_context_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources beyond birth in Palo Alto, California in 1968.
primary_early_advantage_tags: MIT CS, Kerberos team lead, early Linux kernel, Palo Alto origin
evidence_summary: Wikipedia, the /dev/random article, Linux kernel random.c copyright (Theodore Ts'o, 1994), Schneier blog, and BSI Linux RNG analysis independently date /dev/random's creation to Ts'o in 1994. Birth year 1968 implies age ~26. Parallel 1994 ext2 design paper with Card and Tweedie and MIT Kerberos leadership confirm deep systems work by that age. Later FSF award (2006), Linux Foundation CTO role, and Google kernel work came after 26.
starting_point: Born 1968 in Palo Alto, California; family socioeconomic details not documented; trained at MIT in computer science (S.B. 1990).
current_position: Senior Linux kernel and storage engineer at Google; longtime ext4 maintainer and e2fsprogs maintainer; FSF Award for the Advancement of Free Software (2006); RESF board member (2023).

trajectory.event: Graduated MIT with computer science degree and continued at MIT IS on Kerberos development.
Began working with Linux as one of the earliest North American kernel developers.
Created /dev/random kernel CSPRNG interface and co-authored Design and Implementation of the Second Extended Filesystem.
Left MIT IS after leading Kerberos work; later joined VA Linux and then IBM on kernel performance.
Received Free Software Foundation Award for the Advancement of Free Software.
Joined Google to work on kernel, filesystem, and storage (including ext4).

parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a prominent academic biologist; broader family history includes foundational logician George Boole—intellectual capital more than direct neural-network apprenticeship.

name: Ada Lovelace
milestone_by_age_26: Ineligible: Born December 10, 1815; met Charles Babbage and began serious mathematical collaboration from age 17–18, but the material milestone—publication of her translation of Menabrea with extensive Notes A–G (including Note G Bernoulli algorithm) in Taylor's Scientific Memoirs—appeared in August/September 1843 when she was 27. Just after the age-26 cutoff.
early_history_summary: Only legitimate child of Lord Byron and Anne Isabella Milbanke, Lovelace was raised primarily by her mother after Byron left England. Privately tutored in mathematics (William Frend, Mary Somerville, later Augustus De Morgan), she was presented at court at 17, married William King in 1835, and became Countess of Lovelace in 1838. Friendship with Babbage from 1833 led to the 1842–43 Analytical Engine notes.
family_context_summary: Aristocratic Anglo-British family: daughter of poet Lord Byron and reformer Annabella Milbanke; raised with substantial wealth, private tutors, and high-society scientific access despite strained parental relationships and childhood illness.
parent_family_domain_summary: Mother emphasized mathematics education partly to counter Byron's 'poetic' influence; father was literary, not scientific. Domain advantage came more from elite tutoring and social access to Babbage/Somerville than parental STEM careers.
evidence_summary: Wikipedia, Computer History Museum, and Bodleian/ACM historical writing agree Notes published 1843. Age at publication is 27 (turned 27 in December 1842). Meeting Babbage at 18 is formative but not the dated material milestone of recognized success used for eligibility.
